meta.subtitle: FY26 10-K and Q1 FY27 update: the backlog is converting, the free cash flow is not

analystCommentary:
**BUY. Target band $165 to $205. Probability-weighted fair value $175.75 against a last price of $150.15.**

The FY26 10-K, for the fiscal year ended 2026-05-31, closed Oracle's fastest growth year in five: revenue $67.4B, {+ +17.4% +}, operating income $20.8B, diluted EPS $5.83. The quarter that followed extended it. Q1 FY27, ended 2026-08-31 and reported on the September call, delivered revenue of $19.3B, {+ +29.6% +} year over year, at a 35.3% operating margin.

The same two years turned Oracle into a levered builder. FY26 free cash flow was {- -$23.7B -} against operating cash flow of $32.0B. Total debt rose to $156.2B from $104.1B. Management has guided full fiscal year CapEx to $90 billion-$95 billion and said the previously disclosed $20 billion at-the-market equity issuance was completed in entirety during Q1 FY27.

At $150.15 the shares trade at 23.2x trailing earnings and at roughly 13.6x the FY28E EPS of $11.02. Those two multiples describe two different companies. Across 86 analysts the consensus target is $236.52 (+57.5%) and the median $241.00, but the range runs $95.00–$325.00 and the split is Buy 56 · Hold 26 · Sell 4. The width of that range is the honest summary of the debate: the bookings are visible, the return on the capital funding them is not.

We think the operating record is worth more than $150.15 and considerably less than consensus, which is why our band sits far below $236.52 and our bear case sits at the street's own low.

executiveSummary.companyOverview:
### What Oracle sells

Oracle provides products and services that build, run and support enterprise information technology frameworks, delivered through cloud-based, on-premise and hybrid deployment models. The FY26 10-K describes three businesses, each comprised of a single operating segment: cloud and software (formerly referred to as cloud and license), hardware, and services.

The cloud and software business represented 87% of total revenues in fiscal 2026 against 86% in fiscal 2025. The composition has shifted underneath the label: cloud revenues were 51% of total revenues in fiscal 2026 against 43% in fiscal 2025. The portfolio spans the Oracle Fusion Cloud suite covering ERP, EPM, SCM and HCM, the NetSuite application suite, Oracle Database, Java and middleware, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure compute, storage and networking.

Hardware represented 5% of total revenues in each of fiscal 2026 and fiscal 2025, covering Oracle Engineered Systems, servers, storage and the related hardware software. Services, meaning consulting services and customer success services, represented 8% of total revenues in fiscal 2026 against 9% in fiscal 2025; the 10-K states this business has lower margins than the other two.

Revenue is concentrated in the Americas at 63.3% of the FY25 geographic mix, with EMEA at 24.4% and Asia Pacific at 12.3%. Oracle was established in 1977 and is headquartered in Austin, Texas.

thesis.body:
Oracle is converting a large contracted backlog into revenue faster than it is converting that revenue into cash, and the gap is financed.

The conversion is real. Management reported cloud infrastructure revenue of $7.4 billion in Q1 FY27, up 121%, after 93% growth in Q4 FY26, and said it now expects around half of remaining performance obligations to convert into sales over the next 36 months. Consensus carries FY27E revenue of ~$90.1B (+34%) and FY28E revenue of $131.2B, nearly double the FY26 base of $67.4B.

The cost shows in three places. Gross margin fell from 70.5% in FY25 to 65.2% in FY26. Free cash flow went from {- -$0.4B -} in FY25 to {- -$23.7B -} in FY26. Total debt rose from $104.1B to $156.2B across the same two fiscal years, with FY27 CapEx guided to $90 billion-$95 billion.

Our base case is that the conversion happens and the returns are adequate but arrive later than the $236.52 consensus target implies. That leaves the shares worth more than $150.15 and much less than the street's mean, with a genuinely wide distribution on both sides.

catalysts: **RPO conversion into revenue.** Management said remaining performance obligations increased $26 billion from Q4 and that it now expects around half of RPO to convert into sales over the next 36 months. Cloud infrastructure revenue of $7.4 billion in Q1 FY27, up 121% after 93% in Q4 FY26, is the first sizable evidence of that conversion showing up in reported revenue rather than in backlog.

**Delivery against the FY27 consensus.** Consensus carries FY27E revenue of ~$90.1B (+34%). Q1 FY27 revenue of $19.3B, {+ +29.6% +} year over year, is consistent with it. Three more quarters at that rate would validate a growth path that a forward multiple of roughly 13.6x on FY28E EPS of $11.02 does not price.

**Applications attach.** Management reported SaaS growth of 10% in Q1 FY27, with Fusion at 14% and industry applications above 20%, and said customers have over 2,300 AI agents in production, up 90% quarter over quarter. Applications revenue does not carry the data center capital intensity of infrastructure, so a sustained acceleration there improves the blended return on the FY27 build.

**Net cash CapEx running below gross CapEx.** Management said Q1 FY27 CapEx was $28 billion while net cash CapEx, after customer prepayments, was $18 billion, and guided the full year to not more than $70 billion of net cash CapEx against $90 billion-$95 billion gross. If prepayments hold at that proportion, the external financing requirement is smaller than the headline capital line. This is management's characterization; it is not yet visible in a full year of reported free cash flow.

**A re-rating from a depressed base.** The shares are $150.15 against a 52-week range of $114.50–$329.50, with 86 analysts split Buy 56 · Hold 26 · Sell 4 and a median target of $241.00. Evidence that the build is earning a return could move the multiple well before it moves reported earnings.
risks: **Financing the build.** Total debt rose to $156.2B in FY26 from $104.1B in FY25, and net debt to $124.9B from $93.3B. FY26 free cash flow was {- -$23.7B -} on an FCF margin of {- -35.2% -}. FY27 CapEx is guided to $90 billion-$95 billion. The 10-K lists risks associated with our outstanding and future indebtedness among its financial risks.

**Dilution and the preferred claim.** Management said the previously disclosed $20 billion at-the-market equity issuance was completed in entirety during Q1 FY27. The 10-K warns that conversion of the 6.50% Series D Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock, payment of its dividends in shares of common stock, or issuance under the ATM Program will dilute the ownership interest of the holders of common stock.

**Margin structure moves against the mix.** Gross margin fell in every year shown, from 79.1% in FY22 to 65.2% in FY26. Management said the Q1 FY27 gross margin decline was expected and driven by ramping up data centers and the acceleration of infrastructure revenue. The more infrastructure succeeds, the lower the blended gross margin goes.

**Capacity execution.** The 10-K warns that if we are unable to secure data center capacity at affordable rates or do not accurately plan for and manage our infrastructure capacity requirements, our profitability may decline. Converting RPO into revenue depends on capacity arriving on schedule and at a planned cost.

**What this pack does not show.** Cloud revenues were 51% of total revenues in fiscal 2026 and cloud infrastructure grew 121% in Q1 FY27, but the facts available here carry no customer concentration disclosure for that infrastructure revenue. The durability of the largest contracts cannot be assessed from what is in front of us.

financials.incomeCommentary:
### FY26, and the quarter after it

The FY26 10-K covers the fiscal year ended 2026-05-31. Revenue was $67.4B, {+ +17.4% +}, the fastest of the five years shown and a step up from +8.4% in FY25 and +6.0% in FY24. Operating income was $20.8B against $17.7B, EBITDA $32.1B against $23.9B, net income $17.1B against $12.4B, and diluted EPS $5.83 against $4.34.

The quality of that growth is mixed. Gross margin was 65.2% in FY26, down from 70.5% in FY25 and from 79.1% in FY22. Operating income grew more slowly than EBITDA, which is the signature of a rising depreciation load from newly built data centers. Net income still grew faster than revenue, so there is real operating leverage below the gross line.

Q1 FY27 is a different period and reads better. The quarter ended 2026-08-31 and was reported on the September call: revenue $19.3B, {+ +29.6% +} year over year, at a 35.3% operating margin against a trailing twelve month operating margin of 32.5%. Management said total revenue grew sequentially in a first quarter for the first time, that cloud infrastructure revenue was $7.4 billion and up 121%, and that cloud apps were up 10%.

Two cautions on the quarter. Management's operating income of $8.2 billion, {+ +31% +}, its roughly flat operating margin of 42%, and its EPS of $1.92, {+ +30% +}, are non-GAAP figures from the call and are not on the same basis as the fiscal year table above. And the 10-K itself warns that quarterly results of operations may fluctuate significantly, in part because the timing of a few large software license transactions is recognized at a point in time.
financials.balanceCommentary:
### A balance sheet rebuilt around the build

At FY26 year end Oracle held $31.9B of cash and short-term investments against $11.2B a year earlier, and total debt of $156.2B against $104.1B. Net debt was $124.9B, up from $93.3B in FY25 and from $54.5B in FY22. Total equity moved from -$5.8B in FY22 to $43.1B in FY26, so the equity deficit of four years ago has been closed; the leverage now sits against assets under construction.

The current ratio improved to 1.12 from 0.75, helped by the cash build. That cash is not spare capital. Management guided FY27 CapEx to $90 billion-$95 billion, with not more than $70 billion of net cash CapEx, after $28 billion of CapEx in Q1 FY27 alone. The FY26 closing cash balance of $31.9B covers a fraction of one year of that program, which is why the funding mix matters more here than the liquidity ratios do.

Management said the previously disclosed $20 billion at-the-market equity issuance was completed in entirety during Q1 FY27. The 10-K names indebtedness as a financial risk and warns that conversion of the 6.50% Series D Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock, payment of its dividends in shares of common stock, or issuance under the ATM Program will dilute the ownership interest of the holders of common stock. With ~2.88B shares outstanding and a market cap of $432.5B, equity raised near $150.15 costs the existing holder considerably more than equity raised near the $329.50 top of the 52-week range.
financials.cashflowCommentary:
### The cash flow statement is the whole argument

Operating cash flow was $32.0B in FY26 against $20.8B in FY25, the best of the five years shown. Free cash flow was {- -$23.7B -}, an FCF margin of {- -35.2% -}, following {- -$0.4B -} in FY25 and a positive $11.8B in FY24. Oracle has now spent two consecutive fiscal years turning a growing operating cash flow into a negative free cash flow.

The quarter moved in the same direction at a better ratio. Management reported record cash flow from operations of $23 billion in Q1 FY27, CapEx of $28 billion, negative free cash flow of $5 billion, and net cash CapEx of $18 billion after customer prepayments.

Management's framing is that the newest backlog is funded differently. It said the vast majority of the contracts added in the quarter were via prepay or bring your own hardware or similar mechanic and so will not require incremental capital from Oracle, and that this new RPO will not impact CapEx or revenues until fiscal 2028 or beyond. Take the claim at face value and it still only describes new RPO. It does not reduce the $90 billion-$95 billion of FY27 CapEx already guided, and that spending is what produces this year's free cash flow deficit.

The practical test for a shareholder is unchanged: free cash flow has to turn before the debt compounds into the equity story. Neither FY26 nor Q1 FY27 shows that turn.

valuation.multiplesCommentary:
### What the price already assumes

At $150.15 Oracle trades at 23.2x trailing earnings, 6.0x sales, 14.7x EV/EBITDA, and 18.5x forward NTM earnings. Against FY28E EPS of $11.02 the forward multiple is roughly 13.6x. The trailing 23.2x and the FY28 13.6x describe two different companies: the price is broadly consistent with FY26 earnings of $5.83 per diluted share and inconsistent with the FY28 consensus.

One of the two has to give. Either FY28E revenue of $131.2B and EPS of $11.02 are too high, or $150.15 is too low. The street does not resolve it either. 86 analysts carry a consensus target of $236.52 (+57.5%) and a median of $241.00, but the range runs $95.00–$325.00 and the ratings split Buy 56 · Hold 26 · Sell 4.

Two qualifications on the multiples themselves. EV/EBITDA of 14.7x rests on an EBITDA base of $32.1B that excludes the depreciation of a capital program still being built, so it flatters a balance sheet carrying $124.9B of net debt. And no peer column is available in this pack, so every multiple here is judged against Oracle's own history rather than against a comparable set.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: RPO converts on management's schedule. Around half of remaining performance obligations convert into sales over the next 36 months as management describes, cloud infrastructure growth stays near the 121% posted in Q1 FY27, and FY28E revenue of $131.2B with EPS of $11.02 is met. Prepay and bring-your-own-hardware contracts hold net cash CapEx at or below the guided $70 billion, so free cash flow inflects during fiscal 2028 without a further equity raise. On that record the multiple re-rates past the median street target of $241.00.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: The growth lands and the cash return arrives late. FY27E revenue of ~$90.1B (+34%) is broadly met, FY28E EPS of $11.02 is approached rather than hit, capacity comes online on a slower schedule, and gross margin stays nearer the 65.2% of FY26 than the 70.5% of FY25. Free cash flow remains negative through FY27 against the $90 billion-$95 billion CapEx guide, and debt above the FY26 level of $156.2B caps the multiple Oracle can earn. The shares work from $150.15, but nowhere near the +57.5% the $236.52 consensus target implies.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: Capacity or credit binds first. Cloud infrastructure growth decelerates sharply from 121%, the newest RPO, which management said will not impact revenues until fiscal 2028 or beyond, converts later and thinner than assumed, and FY28E revenue of $131.2B proves far too high. Further years of negative free cash flow after the {- -$23.7B -} of FY26 force more issuance under the ATM Program or more preferred, with total debt already $156.2B. The common equity absorbs the gap and the price lands at $95.00, the bottom of the street's $95.00–$325.00 target range and below the $114.50 52-week low.

valuation.scenarioCommentary:
### How the band is built

The three cases weight to a fair value of $175.75 against the $150.15 last price. The target band is $165 to $205 and brackets the $180 base case. That is a BUY, and it sits far below the +57.5% implied by the $236.52 consensus target.

The heaviest weight is on Base, because that is what the evidence supports. Q1 FY27 delivered $19.3B of revenue, {+ +29.6% +}, with cloud infrastructure at $7.4 billion and 121% growth. That is conversion, not just bookings. But FY26 free cash flow of {- -$23.7B -} and FY27 CapEx guidance of $90 billion-$95 billion mean the shareholder is funding that conversion, and the return on the funding is not yet in any reported figure.

The bear weight is close to a third, heavier than the Buy 56 · Hold 26 · Sell 4 analyst split would suggest. Two facts justify it. Total debt is $156.2B against total equity of $43.1B. And the 52-week range of $114.50–$329.50 shows how much multiple this equity can lose inside a single year. The $95.00 bear price is not an invented floor; it is the bottom of the street's own target range.

Bull carries the lightest weight of the three. The mechanism is plausible and management has described it in detail, but it requires both the revenue and the cash to arrive, and only the revenue is currently in evidence.

segments.name: Cloud And License Business
segments.body:
85.8% of the FY25 revenue mix at $49.2B. The FY26 10-K renames it cloud and software, formerly referred to as cloud and license, and puts it at 87% of total revenues in fiscal 2026 against 86% in fiscal 2025.

Two very different economics sit inside the one segment. Software support is the durable half: the 10-K states that substantially all software support customers renew their support contracts with us upon expiration, that those contracts are priced as a percentage of the net fees paid for the license, billed in advance, and recognized ratably over a term that is generally one year. Oracle Cloud Infrastructure is the other half, with Q1 FY27 revenue of $7.4 billion growing 121% and carrying the data center cost base that took gross margin from 70.5% in FY25 to 65.2% in FY26.

Cloud revenues reached 51% of total revenues in fiscal 2026 against 43% in fiscal 2025, so the second half is becoming the larger one. Anyone underwriting this segment today is underwriting the infrastructure economics, not the support annuity.

segments.name: Hardware Business
segments.body:
5.1% of the FY25 revenue mix at $2.9B, and 5% of total revenues in each of fiscal 2026 and fiscal 2025 per the 10-K. The range covers Oracle Engineered Systems, servers, storage, industry-specific hardware offerings, and the operating system, virtualization and management software sold with them, the majority through independent distributors and value-added resellers.

The 10-K is candid that quarterly hardware revenues are difficult to predict, and names among the causes its manufacturing partners' ability to deliver a few large transactions, customer demand for competing cloud infrastructure offerings, and the effect of tariffs and other trade barriers on costs. Hardware support is the steadier piece, priced as a percentage of the net hardware products fees and recognized ratably over a term that is generally one year.

At this size the segment does not move the equity. It matters as a cost and trade-policy exposure, and as a reminder that Oracle still carries a physical supply chain alongside the cloud build.

segments.name: Services Business
segments.body:
9.1% of the FY25 revenue mix at $5.2B, and 8% of total revenues in fiscal 2026 against 9% in fiscal 2025 per the 10-K. The business is consulting services and customer success services, formerly referred to as advanced customer services, recognized over time as the services are performed.

The filing states plainly that this business has lower margins than the cloud and software and hardware businesses, and that its costs are primarily personnel-related, with technology infrastructure, facilities and external contractor expenses alongside. Its revenue is derivative: the 10-K ties services demand to customer demand for the cloud and software and hardware offerings that the services attach to.

Management said that at AI World in October it will unveil an agentic AI accelerator intended to compress SaaS deployments from years to months, and months to weeks. If it works as described, it would reduce the implementation hours a customer needs to buy. That is a claim about a product not yet shown; the fall in this segment's share of revenue in fiscal 2026 is the only evidence available here.

moatFactors.name: Software support renewals
moatFactors.body: The 10-K states that substantially all software support customers renew their support contracts with us upon expiration, in order to continue to benefit from technical support services and the periodic issuance of unspecified updates and enhancements. Support is priced as a percentage of the net fees paid for the license, billed in advance of the service being performed, and recognized ratably. This annuity is the most predictable revenue Oracle has, and it is what funded a gross margin of 79.1% in FY22.

moatFactors.name: Database and Java installed base
moatFactors.body: The infrastructure technologies the 10-K names, Oracle Database, Java, middleware, the Oracle Autonomous Database and MySQL HeatWave, sit underneath customer applications and are costly to displace. The filing's own description of its migration programs, which let customers pivot their licenses and the related software support to the Oracle Cloud and expand with it for existing workloads, shows the installed base working as a channel into the cloud rather than as a stranded legacy asset.

moatFactors.name: Fusion suite breadth
moatFactors.body: Oracle sells ERP, EPM, SCM and HCM as one Oracle Fusion Cloud suite, alongside NetSuite and industry applications. Management reported Fusion growing 14% and industry applications above 20% in Q1 FY27, against SaaS overall at 10%. Suite breadth raises switching costs, but it does not prevent share loss module by module, and the 10% aggregate is the fairer measure of how fast the suite is actually winning.

moatFactors.name: Cloud infrastructure scale
moatFactors.body: Cloud revenues reached 51% of total revenues in fiscal 2026 from 43% in fiscal 2025, and management reported cloud infrastructure revenue of $7.4 billion in Q1 FY27, up 121% after 93% in Q4 FY26. Scale in infrastructure is bought rather than accumulated, and the 10-K names the inability to secure data center capacity at affordable rates as a distinct threat to profitability. We treat this as the weakest of the four moat sources even though it is the fastest growing.

businessMoat.durability:
We rate the moat WIDE, but the rating rests on the old business rather than the new one. The 10-K's statement that substantially all software support customers renew, set against a database and Java installed base embedded in customer systems, gives Oracle pricing power that does not depend on the current capital program at all. That half of the company would still be here if cloud infrastructure growth halved.

The new half is different in kind. Cloud infrastructure competes on capacity, price and delivery schedule, and the 10-K lists both the risk of being unable to secure data center capacity at affordable rates and the risk of being unable to compete effectively. The margin evidence is already in the accounts: gross margin fell from 70.5% in FY25 to 65.2% in FY26 as infrastructure mix rose, and cloud revenues went from 43% to 51% of total revenues over the same two fiscal years.

The honest summary is that Oracle is spending an entrenched franchise's cash flow to buy a position in a business with a narrower moat than the one it already owns. That can be the right trade at the right price. It is not the same trade the WIDE rating on its own would imply.

points: **The five-year record.** Revenue grew from $42.4B in FY22 to $67.4B in FY26, with annual growth of +17.7%, +6.0%, +8.4% and {+ +17.4% +}. The middle of that run is the relevant base rate: Oracle spent two of the last four fiscal years growing in single digits. The reacceleration is recent and infrastructure-driven, not a long-standing trend.

**What consensus now requires.** FY27E revenue of ~$90.1B (+34%), then FY28E revenue of $131.2B, nearly double the FY26 base of $67.4B. Q1 FY27 revenue of $19.3B, {+ +29.6% +}, is a start consistent with the first of those years. Nothing in the reported record yet speaks to the second.

**Where the growth actually sits.** Cloud revenues were 51% of total revenues in fiscal 2026 against 43% in fiscal 2025, and management reported cloud infrastructure growing 121% in Q1 FY27 after 93% in Q4 FY26 while cloud apps grew 10%. Nearly all the incremental growth is in the capital-intensive half of the business.

**Backlog as the forward indicator.** Management said RPO increased $26 billion from Q4, that around half of RPO should convert into sales over the next 36 months, and that the newest contracts will not affect CapEx or revenues until fiscal 2028 or beyond. RPO is contracted, not delivered, and the 10-K warns that quarterly results may fluctuate significantly. It should be read as a probability-weighted pipeline rather than as revenue.

**The AI usage evidence.** Management reported embedded AI capabilities used more than 150 million times in Q1 FY27 with usage growing 42% sequentially, AI agents executed more than 3.5 million times, over 2,300 AI agents in production and up 90% quarter over quarter, and 900 billion tokens consumed across Fusion. These are usage counts management disclosed. No attach rate, price or revenue contribution is given here, so they evidence engagement rather than monetization.

management.leadership:
### Leadership

The FY26 10-K identifies the chief operating decision makers as our Chief Executive Officers and Chief Technology Officer, so Oracle runs a co-chief-executive structure with the Chief Technology Officer sharing authority over how resources are allocated across the three businesses.

On the September call management described the quarter in one word, acceleration, and pointed to total revenue growing sequentially in a first quarter for the first time. The Q1 FY27 numbers support the headline: revenue $19.3B, {+ +29.6% +}, operating margin 35.3%, and cloud infrastructure revenue of $7.4 billion up 121%.

Management is also making forward claims that cannot be checked against anything in this pack: that around half of RPO converts into sales within 36 months, that acceleration should continue through the remainder of fiscal 2027, and that an agentic AI accelerator to be unveiled in October will compress SaaS deployments from years to months. We record these as management claims rather than as facts. The test we would apply over the next several quarters is whether free cash flow follows the revenue, because the reported record currently shows the two moving apart.
management.capitalAllocation:
### Capital allocation

Capital is going into capacity. Management guided FY27 CapEx to $90 billion-$95 billion with not more than $70 billion of net cash CapEx, after $28 billion of CapEx in Q1 FY27 alone. FY26 operating cash flow was $32.0B. The gap is being funded with debt and equity: total debt reached $156.2B in FY26 from $104.1B in FY25, and management said the previously disclosed $20 billion at-the-market equity issuance was completed in entirety during Q1 FY27.

Shareholder returns continue in the background rather than in the foreground. The dividend yields 1.33% at $150.15, and the 10-K refers to a stock repurchase program while cautioning that it cannot guarantee the program will be fully implemented or that it will enhance long-term stockholder value.

The allocation is coherent but unhedged. Oracle is trading the 79.1% gross margin profile it carried in FY22 for the 65.2% it reported in FY26, financed with leverage, in exchange for a far larger revenue base. If FY28E revenue of $131.2B arrives, the trade works. If it does not, the $156.2B of debt remains either way.
management.governance:
### Governance

The capital structure has become the governance story. The 10-K discloses 6.50% Series D Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock and related depositary shares, an At the Market equity program, and warns that conversion of the Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock and the depositary shares, or the payment of dividends on that preferred in shares of common stock, or the issuance of shares under the ATM Program, will dilute the ownership interest of the holders of common stock. It states separately that the common stock ranks junior to the Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock with respect to the payment of dividends and to amounts payable in the event of liquidation, winding-up or dissolution.

That is a real change in what a common holder owns. A preferred instrument carrying a 6.50% coupon ranks ahead of the common, whose dividend yields 1.33% at $150.15, and the ATM Program was used in size during Q1 FY27.

The filing also flags that the ATM Program, the Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock or the depositary shares may adversely affect the market price of the common stock, and that the company cannot guarantee the ATM Program will be fully implemented. The disclosure is clear and specific. It is the terms, not the disclosure, that a common holder needs to price.

idiosyncratic: **Funding risk is the first-order risk.** FY26 free cash flow was {- -$23.7B -} on a margin of {- -35.2% -}, the second consecutive negative year after {- -$0.4B -} in FY25. Total debt is $156.2B and net debt $124.9B. FY27 CapEx is guided at $90 billion-$95 billion. Oracle has to retain access to debt and equity markets on acceptable terms across a multi-year build, and the 10-K lists risks associated with our outstanding and future indebtedness among its financial risks. Management's prepay and bring-your-own-hardware framing describes new RPO and does not retire the FY27 spending already guided.

**Capacity execution.** The 10-K warns that if we are unable to secure data center capacity at affordable rates or do not accurately plan for and manage our infrastructure capacity requirements, our profitability may decline. Converting RPO into revenue depends on capacity arriving on schedule at a planned cost. A slip shows up twice, as revenue that does not recognize and as capital already committed.

**Margin compression as the mix shifts.** Gross margin fell in each of the five years shown: 79.1%, 72.8%, 71.4%, 70.5%, 65.2%. Management said the Q1 FY27 decline was expected and driven by ramping up data centers and the acceleration of infrastructure revenue, offset in the quarter by lower operating costs. The structural point stands: revenue beats and gross margin beats are unlikely to arrive in the same quarter.

**Dilution and the preferred claim.** Management said the $20 billion at-the-market equity issuance was completed in entirety during Q1 FY27. The 10-K warns that conversion of the 6.50% Series D Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock, dividends on it paid in shares of common stock, or further issuance under the ATM Program will dilute common holders, and that the common stock ranks junior to that preferred. With ~2.88B shares outstanding, further issuance nearer the $114.50 low of the 52-week range would cost existing holders far more than issuance nearer the $329.50 high.

**Evidence gaps in this pack.** No customer concentration, no total RPO figure, no segment operating margins and no peer multiple column are available here. Cloud infrastructure revenue of $7.4 billion in Q1 FY27 comes from management's remarks on the September call, not from a segment disclosure in the FY26 10-K. Our conclusions about infrastructure durability therefore rest on thinner evidence than our conclusions about the support annuity.
risks.systemic:
### Systemic risk

Oracle's FY27 plan is a levered position on one macro condition: that demand for AI compute stays strong enough, for long enough, to absorb $90 billion-$95 billion of capacity at prices that earn a return. That condition sits outside Oracle's control. The 10-K's general risks state that economic, political and market conditions can adversely affect the business, results of operations and financial condition, including revenue growth and profitability, which in turn could adversely affect the stock price.

Interest rates matter more here than they did two years ago. Net debt of $124.9B, against $54.5B in FY22, has to be refinanced into whatever credit market exists when the maturities fall due. A funding market that stays open on today's terms is an assumption inside our base case, not a fact in the filing.

Two further exposures are named in the filing. Currency: changes in currency exchange rates can adversely affect customer demand, revenues and profitability, which is relevant with EMEA at 24.4% and Asia Pacific at 12.3% of the FY25 geographic mix. Trade: the 10-K repeatedly cites tariffs and trade policy as factors on both customer demand and the cost of hardware and infrastructure components.

body:
### Recommendation

**BUY. Target band $165 to $205. Probability-weighted fair value $175.75 against a last price of $150.15.**

The judgment is narrower than the label sounds. Oracle is demonstrably converting backlog into revenue: FY26 revenue of $67.4B at {+ +17.4% +}, then Q1 FY27 revenue of $19.3B at {+ +29.6% +} with cloud infrastructure at $7.4 billion and 121% growth. That is a better operating record than a price of $150.15, at 23.2x trailing earnings and roughly 13.6x FY28E EPS of $11.02, reflects.

What stops us going further is the cash flow statement. Free cash flow was {- -$23.7B -} in FY26 and negative $5 billion in Q1 FY27 on management's own numbers, total debt is $156.2B, and FY27 CapEx is guided at $90 billion-$95 billion. Until free cash flow turns, the revenue growth is being bought rather than earned, and the price paid for it is not yet measurable in any reported figure. That is why we sit far below the $236.52 consensus target, and why our bear case carries close to a third of the weight at $95.00, the bottom of the street's own $95.00–$325.00 range.

How we would be proven wrong, in either direction. Bullish: two or three quarters in which cloud infrastructure growth holds near the 121% of Q1 FY27 while net cash CapEx tracks below the guided $70 billion, pulling free cash flow toward breakeven ahead of the fiscal 2028 RPO conversion management describes. Bearish: a quarter in which infrastructure growth decelerates sharply, or in which CapEx guidance rises above the $90 billion-$95 billion range, either of which would force further issuance under an ATM Program already used in full once. We would revisit the band on either.
